items.title: Westchester Knicks 2026-27 Season Primer
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
New York’s G League affiliate opens its 2026-27 season tonight against the Maine Celtics in the Tip-Off Tournament. The roster features three players on two-way contracts, a returning fan favorite (hint: he’s great on toast), and a collection of prospects hoping to dribble their way up to an NBA court.

With the Knicks operating near the second apron, Westchester provides a way to develop young players without committing additional standard roster spots. Two-way players can spend most of the season in White Plains while remaining available for NBA duty, subject to a limit of up to 50 games on the active roster. The G League has also given players like Deuce McBride and Tyler Kolek opportunities to get more work. Here’s a peek at the players worth watching.

Dalton Knecht: A second chance in New York

Of everyone on Westchester’s roster, Dalton Knecht has the clearest path to helping the big club this season. The 2024 first-round pick (17th overall) arrived after the Lakers waived him, with New York releasing Kevin McCullar Jr. to make room for Knecht on a two-way contract. This low-risk move could pay off if the former Tennessee star rediscovers his shooting touch and improves his court awareness, which was a criticism raised in the comments section at Silver Screen and Roll.

The 25-year-old made a promising debut for the New York Knicks this week, scoring 10 points on efficient 4-of-6 shooting (including two threes) with seven boards, a dime, and a block in 16 minutes off the bench in a rout of the Bulls. Finding consistent playing time will be difficult, however. With Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby, Josh Hart, Landry Shamet, Pacôme Dadiet, and Mohamed Diawara competing for minutes on the wings, Knecht will probably need an injury or another opening to receive an extended look. (TBH, he already looks ahead of Dadiet.)

Coach Mike Brown has said he’d rather see Knecht playing meaningful minutes in the G League than sitting on the NBA bench. Makes sense. Knecht needs opportunities to shoot, make decisions, and work through mistakes. He has shown he can score, but questions remain about his defense, shot selection, and ability to contribute consistently as a role player.

If Knecht performs well enough, the organization could eventually consider converting him to a standard NBA contract, which would require sufficient roster and financial room. For now, he should get plenty of opportunities to let it fly against G League competition.

Speaking of flamethrowers . . . Tyler “Silent K” Nickel might be the most straightforward fit for what the Knicks need. New York selected the Vanderbilt sharpshooter with the 47th pick in the 2026 NBA Draft after an impressive senior season. He followed that with a promising Summer League showing and signed a two-way contract.

From what we’ve seen, Nickel moves well without the ball, finds open space, and punishes defenses for leaving him unattended. The big league Knicks have several players capable of creating offense, and a dependable perimeter shooter who doesn’t require many touches could fit nicely alongside them (see: Landry Shamet).

His defense will help determine how quickly the 23-year-old advances. He needs to prove he can handle quicker, stronger NBA bodies while maintaining his shooting efficiency against more aggressive closeouts. Westchester should give him plenty of reps to work on both.

Nickel doesn’t seem to have Knecht’s offensive versatility, but his shooting gives him a clearly defined role. If he can hold his own defensively, he could become a useful option for additional spacing. For the time being, Westchester might have its very own set of Splash Brothers to keep you entertained (at a reasonable price).

Jaden Akins: Defense and versatility

Jaden Akins took a less direct route to New York. Undrafted out of Michigan State in 2025, he spent last season with the Motor City Cruise after earning All-Big Ten third-team and All-Defensive recognition as a senior. His combination of scoring, secondary playmaking, and defense caught the Knicks’ attention. Westchester acquired his returning player rights in September, and he secured a two-way contract before the season.

Akins faces considerable competition at the one- and two-guard spots. His best chance of separating himself is to use his time at Westchester to polish his defense and his work off the ball. Can he defend multiple positions, run an offense for stretches, and make open shots? Can he contribute consistently without committing unnecessary fouls or turnovers? Those qualities will probably matter more to New York than his individual scoring averages.

Dink Pate: Back for another season

The fan favorite returns! Dink Pate returns to Westchester after a confusing offseason. The 6’8” wing, still only 20 years old, averaged approximately 16 points, seven rebounds, and four assists across 50 games with the club last season. He subsequently attempted to play college basketball at Providence, but that plan fell through amid questions about his NCAA eligibility. The Knicks signed and waived him on an Exhibit 10 contract, and he returned to Westchester, which already held his G League rights.

Pate has length, can create his own offense, and contributes as a rebounder and passer. His combination of physical tools and professional experience makes him one of Westchester’s more interesting developmental players. Decision-making and efficiency are where he needs improvement.

Unlike Knecht, Nickel, and Akins, Pate doesn’t have a two-way contract. He would need an available two-way or standard roster spot and a new NBA contract to join the big club. Westchester’s rights also don’t prevent another NBA team from signing him. Thus, his time in White Plains is a prove-it run for a broader audience—so we expect to see some inspired hooping from him this season.

Frontcourt depth: Robbins, Dante, and Miličić

Westchester’s frontcourt includes several players who could provide useful depth. , a seven-footer who went undrafted out of Vanderbilt in 2023, is probably the most recognizable. He showed some encouraging work around the iron during Summer League with the Knicks, and Westchester subsequently acquired his G League rights.

Robbins brings size, rebounding, and shot-blocking ability. The big league club could use more reliable center depth behind Karl-Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond, with James Wiseman slow to make an impression. Robbins could use his time in White Plains to convince the team he deserves a look—perhaps before the front office starts eyeing its surplus of guards as trade bait.

, the 6-foot-11 former Oregon center, is working his way back from an ACL injury. His size and athleticism lift our eyebrows, but getting healthy and regaining his previous form will be the immediate priorities.

, a 6-foot-10 forward out of Tennessee, brings international experience and positional versatility after spending time with the Delaware Blue Coats last season. Improving his outside shooting and defensive consistency would help him take the next step.

The wings: Jourdain, Okani, and company

Westchester also has several forwards competing for rotation minutes. returns after averaging roughly eight points and more than five rebounds last season. The former Memphis forward provides rebounding, energy, and defensive effort. His journey from local tryout to returning player is a nice story, even if an NBA opportunity remains a longer shot.

, the former West Virginia wing, brings length and athleticism after spending time with multiple G League organizations. , an undrafted forward out of Duquesne, and are also trying to establish roles after joining the training camp group.

The guards: Shooting potential

Westchester’s backcourt includes several capable players. is worth watching after arriving from the Stockton Kings. The 6’5” guard shot approximately 42% from downtown last season, giving Westchester another option to stretch the floor.

returns as a scoring option at guard and on the wing, while joins the club after being selected 25th in the 2026 G League Draft. Spears brings extensive college experience, including a productive stint at UTSA, and spent last season playing professionally in Mexico.

The three two-way players will receive the most attention this season, although we’ll also keep an eye on Pate (‘cuz he’s kinda electric). The rest of the roster will compete for minutes and try to establish themselves as dependable professional players. Westchester opens its Tip-Off Tournament schedule tonight at 7 p.m. against the Maine Celtics at the Portland Expo, then faces the same opponent at the same venue Sunday at 12:30 p.m. Both games will air on MSG Network.

items.title: The Knicks have a bench guard conundrum
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
When you’re the defending champions, there are not many holistic things to complain about.

Sure, the Knicks started 0-3 with a very unsettling offense, but all they needed was their medicine (the Nets and Bulls) to get back to .500?

Worried about losing to Philadelphia twice in October? Joel Embiid’s plantar fasciitis has already acted up; calm down.

Any “problems” this early in the season are either short-term, regarding the looming extension talks, or good problems, which are more conundrums than actual problems.

The biggest of those conundrums has to do with the Knicks’ rotation, specifically with their copious amounts of guard depth.

Jalen Brunson is the head of the snake, but after him? There are a lot of players with minutes who could fluctuate on any given night.

Tyler Kolek and Jose Alvarado duel over backup ball-handler minutes. Jordan Clarkson and Deuce McBride grapple over bench two-guard minutes. Landry Shamet’s strong play is actively pushing starters Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart over their minutes with the three entrenched parts of the team’s nucleus.

It does qualify as a good problem to have, as injuries will undoubtedly give each of these guys ample opportunity over the course of 82 games, but when they’re all healthy, like they are right now? It probably gives Mike Brown a bigger headache than watching Andre Drummond attempt layups.

All of these guys provide something that the Knicks could use more of, but have warts that can limit their playing time.

Kolek is the best true playmaker, but he’s a poor defender, and his jump shot has been consistent throughout his young NBA career. This basically also describes Alvarado, but the defense is better from the New York native.

McBride has stretches where he’s the team’s best rate shooter and is a tremendously pesky point-of-attack defender… but is that not what the team is getting out of a taller two-guard in Shamet?

Clarkson has been a sparkplug every game he’s played this year, but the 35-year-old showed his maddening inconsistency in his first year in New York.

It’s created an extremely volatile rotation, which isn’t surprising when you have a coach who opened the year saying only five players on this team have minutes that are secured.

Despite zero Knicks players averaging more than 33 minutes a game except Brunson (who’s at 34.1), only Shamet is averaging more than 18 minutes a game off the bench.

McBride is at 17.5, Kolek is at 12.2, Alvarado is at 11.3, and Clarkson is at 9.9, but even these are deceiving.

Kolek has played steady rotation minutes, but didn’t play at all in the first two games before Alvarado’s ankle injury. Alvarado played 16 and 11 minutes, got hurt, got benched after nine minutes on Monday, and was on track to be a DNP-CD against the Bulls on Wednesday.

Clarkson’s gone from playing three, five, or eight minutes to his spurts of 15 and 17 in the two games against the Bulls and his 11 to spark the incredible fourth quarter against Brooklyn.

McBride, who’s served as the Knicks’ sixth man for over two years now, has topped 17 minutes just twice. He played a season-low 11 minutes on Wednesday and hasn’t had a clear role.

To get these guys more minutes, it would mean cutting minutes from Hart or Bridges. While both have their warts, and the latter continues to look somehow less involved than he was during his lowest moments last season, some of the Knicks’ best lineups are coming with them on the court… just separated.

We’ve seen Brown deploy line changes significantly more in the early going, opting to sub in three or four players at a time to deploy uniform units, but that’s not helping how erratic this all feels.

The depth is making players redundant on the court, especially with how unwise it is to run four-guard lineups in an NBA that’s prioritizing size and length more and more.

And with the Knicks’ extremely shallow forward and center depth? This glut might have to be sorted out at the trade deadline. As much as McBride has shown his tremendous value to the Knicks over the course of his contract, if he isn’t going to play more, is it even a net positive to keep him for the playoff run?

For now, it’s merely a conundrum that Coach Brown will be scratching his head over every game.

By the time we hit February? Things better be sorting themselves out.

items.title: Law & Order SVU Watch Along
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Jalen Brunson of the New York Knicks makes his scripted acting debut in Law & Order: SVU Season 28, Episode 5 (“Forsaken”). The show airs tonight at 9 p.m. ET on NBC and will stream on Peacock tomorrow.

Captain Clutch will play Detective Jay Madison (a nod to Madison Square Garden, obvs) across from Knicks superfan Mariska Hargitay (Captain Olivia Benson).  Official synopsis: When a wedding guest is assaulted at the reception, Benson and the squad uncover a secret that changes the course of the investigation; ADA Sonny Carisi’s pursuit of justice is complicated when key witnesses refuse to cooperate.

Tip-off’s at 9. Join us as we watch together. Please don’t post large photos, GIFs, or links to illegal streams in the thread. Treat each other respectfully. And break a leg, Jalen!

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I said it for you, I hope I don’t get in trouble’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
New York was so good on Wednesday that the Knicks made me hate them for effectively finishing my 2-hour night plan in 20 minutes.

I’m cool with the 4-1 in the last five, but let’s make it a bit more competitive for entertainment’s sake, please and thank you (I know I’m in the minority here. Alas)

Here’s everything said before and after yesterday’s bullfighting.

On the entire Knicks roster contributing to the victory over Chicago:

“I take my hat off to everybody on the roster, because everybody contributed in some way, shape or form.”

On the Knicks delivering their most complete performance of the season against Chicago:

“That was as close to a 48-minute game as our group has had yet.”

On the Knicks’ franchise-record-tying 84-point first half:

“It was a really good half, in terms of doing what we believe, what we should be doing offensively as our staples. Everybody was really good in those areas.”

On the Knicks’ spacing, ball movement and offensive execution against Chicago:

“I really liked how we started out. Spacing the floor well, touching the paint, and then re-spacing too. Our re-spacing was really quick and really decisive. We had some great, great looks early on. And everybody played well offensively. Our pace was pretty good, it’s something we’ve been talking about. Our offensive rebounding, for shooting a high percentage, was pretty good. Just a lot of good things.”

On Brunson finally making the shots he had been missing earlier in the season:

“He’s obviously missed some shots but he took the same shots tonight that he’s been taking. And, we felt we’ve gotten some good shots in previous games that just haven’t gone down. But the good part about it is, they went down tonight, and we defended. A great game by him as well as everybody else.”

On Jalen Brunson’s unusual endurance and how the Knicks track player fatigue:

“Our analytics guys [chart] how guys play in two-minute increments. Some guys, after six minutes, their three-point field-goal percentage drops. They also can track their movement — how quickly they’re still moving out on the floor, if that slows down or not. Jalen’s just seems to go up every two minutes.”

On Brunson’s toughness and why he must avoid overworking him before the playoffs:

“He’s about as durable as anybody I’ve been around. He’s mentally tough, physically tough, and he can push himself to go… But at the end of the day, it’s going to impact him, in my opinion, come playoff time, so I have to be conscious of not going to the well too much, especially at this point in the season.”

On why he did not let Brunson continue playing after his 22-point first quarter:

“No, because he played 12 straight minutes.”

On Brunson’s ability to maintain his production over extended playing time:

“Jalen’s numbers just seem to go up every two minutes and there’s really no time when it’s down. So, can he play 12 straight minutes? Yes. Can he play 36-38 minutes? Yes. But, at the end of the day, it’s going to impact him, in my opinion, come playoff time. I have to be conscious not to go to the well too much, especially at this point in the season.”

On Landry Shamet earning playing time through his performances:

“The tough part about it is I don’t remember when that happened last year, but it’s more so the reality [that] Landry is playing well. Landry, he played well in the last game. As you guys can see I’ll try to go with who I think is playing well. I’ll try to find minutes for them . . . Sometimes the other guys are playing good and that’s who you rock with to try to get the win at times.”

On Tyler Kolek replacing Jose Alvarado as the Knicks’ backup point guard:

“I said this before, every position coming off the bench is a competition, all the time. Nobody’s minutes are set in stone. … Jose had the first opportunity in our last game. And then I gave Tyler an opportunity in the second half [against the Nets] and Tyler played well. So I’m gonna go with Tyler. And if I think I need to make a change because Tyler’s not getting it done in my eyes, then I’ll go back to Jose.”

On limiting the Knicks’ starters’ minutes during the first games of the season:

“I don’t want to kill these guys because they played more games — if you’re talking about last season — than most of them had in their career. And the offseason was a lot shorter than what it’s usually been. And it takes a toll. Playing (19) playoff games, it’s a lot different than playing (19) regular-season games. It might be a game-and-a-half just because of how physical the games are and the mental stress that goes into it, the attention to detail in each individual possession.”

On the physical and mental toll of the Knicks’ championship season and balancing rest with winning:

“It can be a mental and physical toll that can impact everybody differently. I have to be careful of not overreacting and trying to lay the hammer, especially early, on every little thing. I got to let our guys breathe a little bit and get their feet underneath them, not just from a physical standpoint, but a mental standpoint as well, because we played a lot of basketball last year and we’re right back to it. I also need to be careful in making sure that I’m not overextending all of our guys early. I wanted to use a 10-man rotation. There were a couple of games I think I went to nine.

“I hate saying this — I want to win, I’m going to try to win, but I’m not going to do that to the detriment of our group later on. So, I’ve got to find the balance of how to use my bench a little better to give these guys some more needed rest during the course in games, so they’re not at 35, 36, 37 minutes right now. I thought that helped us out a lot last year. We’ll up their minutes as the year goes along. I haven’t been too good with that so far this year.”

On adjusting the rotation after the Knicks’ slow start:

“We experimented with different stuff and our players not getting it done caused us to start off a little slow. So, to get us on track, we’re going to hold the fort down with a veteran group of guys.”

On managing the Knicks’ practices and playing time:

“I have to be conscious of how we practice. And I have to try to be conscious of guys’ minutes.”

On calling out his players for losing track of the game at times:

“We hit a three, we celebrated the three and they got a layup on the other end… that’s one of the little things that we talk about embracing playing with next play speed, playing the right way no matter what the score is… (by not doing that), that’s how you build bad habits.”

On Dalton Knecht’s offensive versatility and defensive development:

“He’s a scorer. He’s not just a shooter. A lot of people think he’s a shooter because he’s white. I said it for you, I hope I don’t get in trouble. He can go get it. He can shoot from range, he’s got a medium game, he can get to the rim, and he can pass. He’s got to work defensively and I thought tonight, he tried to play within himself and contributed the best way he could.

“There were a couple things defensively that he can do a little better and that’s what he really has to concentrate on but I thought he gave us a nice little lift, especially offensively when he played towards the end of the first half.”

On the Knicks’ improvement despite their early-season inconsistency:

“You want it, but you can’t live and die by trying to have everything be great and-or perfect in a matter of a week or two weeks. We know we can play better. The crazy part about it is we’re 3-1 in our last four. Knowing that we’re hungry for more, and that strive for perfection is going to help us out when it really counts at the end of the day.

“So we just can’t let go of the rope, we have to keep trying to get better on both sides of the ball and make sure that we’re embracing the little things so that we can hit a groove so we’ll be where we want to be at the end of the season — but knowing that we’re going to go through ups and downs throughout the course of the year.”

On giving starters more opportunities to overcome their struggles than bench players:

“Our starters are going to get a lot more rope than the guy’s coming off the bench, you know? And that’s kind of how I look at it. Again, this is a process and I have to always be careful of not trying to want [perfection]. You want it, but you can’t live and die by trying to have everything be great and/or perfect in a matter of a week or two weeks.”

On finding his rhythm and creating offense through defense:

“Obviously, making 3s, but I think making our two-pointers are really important as well. When you have it going, it feels good. Just trying to play off that and use your gravity to make plays. I feel like it really started on the defensive side of the ball, we were able to get stops and get out in transition.”

On using his scoring gravity to get teammates involved:

“When you have it going, it feels good. And then just trying to play off that and using my gravity to get teammates involved.”

On whether he would ask Mike Brown to leave him in a game to pursue an exceptional scoring performance:

“Possibly, but it has to be the right moment, right time. I don’t want to say no because you never know when you’re in this situation, but I just want to respect the game as much as possible.”

On the Knicks’ defensive effort setting up their offensive breakout against Chicago:

“I feel like it started on the defensive side of the ball. We were able to get stops and get out in transition, create a comfortable lead, and I think we played well with the lead for the most part.”

On the Knicks’ familiarity with their Eastern Conference rivals and the advantage of roster continuity:

“I think everyone in the East knows each other. This is our third year now with each other, so you know, it’s rare. That’s one of our advantages.”

On comparing the current Knicks to LeBron James and the Miami Heat’s Big Three era:

“At the end of the day, people knew, when LeBron and the Big Three were there, you had to go out there and beat them. Everyone brings their best against the New York Knicks. You’ve got to protect the jersey, the city at all costs.”

On handling the distractions and pressure of playing in New York:

“I mean, we did it all last year. You’re in New York, you’ve got to play through distractions; that’s what comes with playing here. There’s a lot of pressure, a lot of noise.”

On the Knicks’ ability to accomplish something special by staying united:

“But as long as this locker room, which has shown it can do, stays together and continues to just believe and fall into each other when things get tough, we can do something special.”

On how the Knicks grew closer during their difficult stretch after winning the NBA Cup:

“We didn’t look our best version, and we heard about it. This team continued to fall into each other instead of splitting away and … separating. We got closer and closer.”

On the pressure of playing in New York and how quickly fans’ expectations can change:

“I guarantee you, I’m going to be sitting here rock bottom. I don’t think I’m ever going to be on my high horse, either. We’re in New York. Everything rides on the next game. We go on a 10-game winning streak and the next game we lose, they’re ready to burn the place down. We know what it is. It’s the tough part of being in New York.”

On the Knicks’ short offseason and the physical toll of the championship celebrations:

“We gotta go out there and win games. And we gotta get those championship habits back, because we were away from it for I don’t know how many months. I think it’s a tough spot. It’s kinda like a little conundrum, because obviously we played into mid-June. Then in the summer obviously you’re working out, you’re doing that, but you also are enjoying the fruits of the labor of winning in terms of going to brands, going to appearances. Off the court, it’s kind of booming for you. So, you’re doing all of that, so that takes a little bit of a wear on you. And then you get into it. So sometimes, the body has to kinda catch up.”

On the Knicks’ open communication and willingness to have difficult conversations:

“It’s open. Anybody can step up, whether it’s the [bench] guys or starters. That’s the thing about this team, our chemistry is so good and we have a lot of trust because we see each other putting forth a lot of work.”

On accepting a reduced role and contributing energy even when he isn’t playing:

“[Brown] knows I’m always ready. My teammates know that I’m always ready and am going to try to bring the energy. If that’s not on the stat sheet or paper, just trying to do the little things, that’s something that I’ve grown in since I’ve been here. That really took priority for me.”

On being ready when the Knicks activated him for his debut against Chicago:

“I wasn’t surprised, I just came in ready to go. The coaches said you’re active so that just means be ready.”

On his first Knicks points coming on a putback dunk and making his debut:

“It was great. Honestly I didn’t hear much just because I’m so locked in, but it was good. Pretty much my first play was a putback dunk so it’s cool, it’s great.”

On wanting to contribute as a scorer and defender:

“I think I just go out there and impact the game on all three levels. And I just wanna show on the other side of the ball, getting the ball pressure and stuff like that and going in and grabbing defensive rebounds.”

On staying prepared for opportunities and learning from teammates on the bench:

“Be ready so you don’t have to get ready. Just watching on the bench and talking to my teammates is really helpful and it was easy to get in there and play confident. All the guys out there gave me a good look.”

items.title: Knicks 135, Bulls 105: “We’re so back…”
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
As the second quarter started last night between the New York Knicks and the Chicago Bulls at Madison Square Garden, Josh Giddey was bringing the ball up for the team from the Windy City. He tried to maneuver through a high pick-and-roll when all of a sudden a large human named OG Anunoby appeared in his path. The Australian must have thought he’d run into a boxing kangaroo, as he was so freaked out that he immediately lost his dribble. As the ball was bouncing away from him, Anunoby lunged after it but couldn’t quite grab it. So Mikal Bridges joined the scene as well for the orange and blue, also diving on the floor to ultimately force the refs to call a foul on poor Mr. Giddey.

Just for the record, the Knicks were leading 43-21 at that point.

The game was essentially over long before both of New York’s high-priced wings draped themselves across the shiny Garden floor, but this is exactly what makes the symbolism of the aforementioned play so much more distinct. The Knicks decided to show up last night. They decided to put it together and be the hard-nosed, all-out championship team we all love so much. Not only for the layup lines or the press conference but for the entire game. They not only cut up the Bulls into sirloins, briskets and ribs, they surely also took their hearts. And announced, if not to the league, then to their fan base, what Keef so aptly commented in : “We are so back…”

Knicks play complete game against Chicago

A critical comrade might point out that it had more to do with Chicago being gone than with New York being back, but this isn’t the day for such rationality. It’s a day of basking in the glory of being a good basketball team and showing it for 47 minutes and 58 seconds, maybe even longer. It’s exactly what this Knicks team needed after sluggish weeks to start their championship defense, and some of us fans might have needed it even a bit more. We all knew they were good enough to win it all, we all knew that there’s a level to their quality that might be unrivaled across the Association. At some point you have to see it, though, and we sure did last night.

From Jalen Brunson to Landry Shamet, from OG Anunoby to Mohamed Diawara, even from James Wiseman to Dalton Knecht, there basically was no Knick who didn’t look like his very best last night, at least not if we ignore garbage time and a rusty Jose Alvarado being dealt the thankless job of driving the party boat into the harbor. Maybe our Finals hero was a bit tired from all the clapping and cheering he did for a seemingly gazillion beautiful basketball plays from his teammates—even if SGA Anunoby gave him plenty of breaks standing at the charity stripe. All in all, the Knicks definitely played at a completely different speed than the Bulls, who only a week ago had raced out to a 19-point lead against New York. Watching this game, you wonder how that ever happened.

No matter what conclusion you might come to answering that question, last night proved that it’s a lot more fun to bring your A-game and best effort from the get-go than midway through the fourth, fueled by desperation. Jalen Brunson danced through the Bulls D like he was Barry Sanders playing a high school team early on and also had no mercy shooting the ball. As so often in the past, it inspired his team to follow him. The Knicks did it all the way to the highest-scoring half in their history, tying a 38-year-old franchise record. It’s nice to be back doing historical things just as they routinely did last season. And just like your starters and stars diving on the floor in a lopsided game, it is a reminder that these Knicks are still those Knicks.

Young Knicks make a good impression

Whether they might be even a bit more here or there could start to show itself in games like last night’s laugher. It is here where younger, unproven bench players like Mo Diawara, Dalton Knecht or James Wiseman will get their chances to make an impression on Mike Brown and the coaching staff. All of them have a ways to go, but watching last night, you at least feel a little intrigued by Mo’s and Wiseman’s physical profiles. Their length could give New York a different defensive dimension (5 blocks between them), and Diawara once again looked like the promising role player he teased last season. The herky-jerky is still there, yet he also flashed strong playmaking ability (tied for the team lead with 4 assists) and defensive awareness against supposedly strong wings like Caleb Wilson or Matas Buzelis. Maybe he can be a specialist for matchups like that, who knows? We’ve got 74 games to see more of it and figure out if it can really be a factor in important games.

We’re not going out on a limb saying that it will take some time before the Bulls get to experience such games again. This doesn’t diminish what our Knickerbockers did last night, playing as complete a basketball game as you dare to imagine. As beautiful as some of the passes, shots or dunks were, in the end, the foundation was the little things, many of which are exactly what a large part of the team’s identity is built upon. Things like boxing out your opponent, making the right rotation or flying hard around a screen. Things like making the pass that leads to an assist or pushing the ball when it truly makes sense.

Or diving on the floor after a loose ball, for that matter.

items.title: Knicks 135, Bulls 105: Scenes from the World Champs looking like it
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
After 21 years at our Binghamton mansion, we’re moving. That means Mrs. Russell has countless extra chores for your intrepid blogger, including the retrieval of a loveseat in a sketchy neighborhood just before tip-off of tonight’s game between the Knicks (4-4) and the Bulls (1-7). Planning to watch the game after delivering the furniture to the new mansion (we are fabulously wealthy), I tried to ignore the alerts blowing up my phone. An impossible task. My eye caught “Jalen Brunson is on track to score 76 points” and “84 ties a franchise first-half record,” and all the surprise of tonight’s blowout was spoiled.

What did I see when I finally returned home? Brunson blazin’, OG Anunoby gorging at the free-throw line, KAT recording his eighth straight double-double, a very promising Dalton Knecht debut (10 PTS, 7 RBS, 16 MIN), solid minutes from Diawara, and a 44-point lead with 43% shooting from deep. We’ll need to burn sage around that loveseat to rid the stench of resentment. Final score: 135-105.

Landry Shamet started in place of Josh Hart (sore ankle) and scored the team’s first four points. From there, the Knicks went straight into high gear, turning a 6-6 tie into a 17-8 lead by attacking the paint and shooting with stunning efficiency. Who was the commander of the first-quarter onslaught? Captain Jalen Brunson, scoring his first 14 points on seven shots and finishing the frame with 22. That wasn’t his highest first-quarter total—he dropped 23 on Milwaukee in January 2025. Nonetheless, stunning. Cap had all but six of the Knicks’ first 19 points. Not to be kept in the corner, OG Anunoby contributed seven, including four from the stripe.

Mohamed Diawara checked in around the middle of the quarter, and this time he looked good! The sophomore delivered some of his best minutes yet this season, with a three and a block on Wilson’s layup. Fellow bench buddy Jordan Clarkson added five points, including a sweet transition three (dimed by Brunson). In a flash, the lead reached 22. Karl-Anthony Towns contributed just two points, starting slowly for his second straight game, but he helped in other ways, notching four boards, a steal, and an assist.

What’s your camp: “I Stand with Mikal” or “Mikal’s Got Me Sweating”? The struggling wing did little in the first quarter to calm our nerves about his recent play. He scored no points but dished two dimes and grabbed two boards.

For Chicago, Normal Norman Powell managed four points, while Tre Jones added four off the bench. Chicago got little from its young players, though. Rookie Caleb Wilson must’ve been star-struck in his MSG debut, missing all four of his shots, and Matas Bazookas went scoreless. At the break, the Knicks were sitting on a comfortable 43-21.

Q2: More of the same. Our heroes outscored Chicago 10-5 over the first three minutes to extend their lead to 53-26. The unrelenting Anunoby was still in beast mode, scoring six points and forcing two Josh Giddey turnovers. New York’s 3&D specialist scored 11 points in the quarter to reach 18 by halftime, while his three steals helped keep Chicago twitching and glitching.

With Brunson resting, Tyler Kolek ran the offense effectively, collecting four assists with sweet setups for Bridges, Clarkson, and Shamet. What a wonderful security blanket a skilled playmaker off the bench is. With Kolek dishing, Bridges racked up seven points. Diawara got into the action, too, scoring his first points of the season and finishing with seven first-half points.

Chicago managed a paltry little run early in the period, but New York responded with a 9-4 run that pushed its lead to 62-36—and eventually 78-41 with 1:47 left. Brunson added four points after returning, reaching 26 by halftime, while Towns remained quiet, adding just three more points in the second. You can count on KAT to crash the glass, though, and he did so for two more rebounds, giving him six at halftime. And newest ’Bocker Dalton Knecht made a fine first impression with a putback dunk and a step-back three-pointer for five points.

Chicago’s Josh Giddey had a particularly rough quarter, committing three turnovers in the opening three minutes, although he recovered to finish the half with seven points and four assists. Bahzelis finally got going late, scoring all six of his first-half points in the final 1:06, including a three-pointer with six seconds remaining. Wilson managed five points in the quarter, while Powell added just two, and Chicago found itself bereft of consistent scoring threats or prayers for winning this contest. Halftime score: 84-52. That tied New York’s franchise record for first-half points.

The Knicks had scorched the nets with 63% shooting from the floor and 50% from deep. The Bulls had shot 40% and a grotesque 19% from deep (5-of-26). The good guys also won the rebounding battle, 23-17, despite surrendering eight offensive rebounds, and committed just five turnovers to Chicago’s eight. Weirdly, the Bulls actually outscored the Knicks in the paint, 30-26, and attempted 13 more shots, yet trailed by 32 at halftime. Math was not my strong subject, but that doesn’t compute. Anyhoo, on to the second half!

Yet again, KAT pepped it up at halftime and came out firing. He drilled consecutive three-pointers in the opening minute as the home team goosed its lead to 36. Towns scored 12 points in the first five minutes of the quarter, including a putback layup, and reached another double-double with 17 points and 12 rebounds before heading to the bench.

Brunson added seven points, including a pull-up three, to reach 33 and call it a night.

The Bulls continued to fumble and bumble. Wilson missed his first three shots of the quarter and committed another turnover. Boozelis scored six points in the period, but the Bulls couldn’t make much headway against New York’s enormous lead. Meanwhile, Deuce McBride provided a spark off the Knicks’ bench, picking off passes from Norman Powell and Wilson before hitting a transition three-pointer that extended New York’s lead to 42. McBride later converted a four-point play, giving him seven points in the quarter, while Mohamed Diawara contributed another blocked shot and continued to provide promising minutes on both ends. Brother, imagine if the Knicks could play Chicago every night. . . .

Tre Jones was Chicago’s most productive player late in the quarter, scoring eight points over the final 2:19, including a three-pointer and three free throws. His unit closed the period on a 12-2 run (the Knicks got a little sloppy), but New York still ended the quarter up 113-79.

Hey! Check out this Knecht kid, blocking Buddy Hield’s layup attempt in the closing seconds. It’s gonna be fun to watch him go on heaters in Westchester.

With the Knicks leading by 34 entering the fourth, the reserves got the run of the joint. Andre Drummond opened the quarter with an alley-oop, while Clarkson and Knecht knocked down threes. James Wiseman made the most of his 10 minutes, finishing with eight points, eight rebounds, and three blocks, including rejections of Giddey, Bewzelis, and Patrick Williams. More of that, please! Pacôme Dadiet added four points. The Bulls briefly cut the deficit to 32, but Wiseman answered with a putback dunk and Knecht followed with a jumper. New York’s offense slowed with the end-of-bench guys on the floor, and Chicago won the quarter 26-22, but who’s complaining?

Mo’s knitting a cozy recap to keep you warm. New York travels to Cleveland for a clash with the Cavs. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

items.title: Game Discussion Thread: Knicks vs. Bulls, November 4, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Knicks (3–4) host the Chicago Bulls (1–6) tonight at Madison Square Garden. A win would bring New York .500 and give them two wins over Chicago in eight days. As of this writing, Josh Hart (ankle) is ruled out and Bulls center Nic Claxton (hamstring) is questionable. The Knicks are double-digit favorites against a Bulls team that’s dropped five straight and gives up a league-worst 128.9 points per game.

Fun fact: Ten years ago tonight, Derrick Rose and Joakim Noah returned to Chicago as Knicks and beat the Bulls 117–104 on the day of the Cubs’ World Series parade. Tip-off is 7:30 pm EST on MSG and NBA League Pass. This is your game thread. This is Blog a Bull. Please don’t post large photos, GIFs, or links to illegal streams in the thread. Mind yo’ manners. Go Knicks!

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I’m a little excited that we’re struggling’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
New York hosts the 1-6 Bulls tonight for their second game in a week after beating them last Wednesday.

Chicago is not a team the Knicks should be too worried about, but hey, this is a matchup between sub-.500 teams, so who knows what will happen then and there.

Here’s some of what we heard from the Knicks heading into today’s game.

On a mediocre start to the season:

“Everything can get better… I’m not pissed about the start or upset about the start. There’s a part of me… I’m a little excited that we’re struggling. I want to see if we, right now, can figure it out.

“When you go through the offseason that we went through, everybody celebrates you the way that this lovely city did and the fans of the New York Knicks did, you want to be shaken and brought back to earth right away when the season starts because that grounds you.

“Right now, because we’re not playing our best basketball, we’re seeing some of the challenges that we need to work on. Right now we could be winning games, but it could be false reality.”

On Jalen Brunson’s early-season shooting struggles:

“He’s taking the same shots as in the past. In my opinion, he’s just missing shots. He’s taking the right shots. I think all our guys are, for the most part, taking the right shots. Right now, they’re not going in. And that can be for this reason, that reason, I don’t know, and I’m not going to try to overanalyze it. As long as they keep taking the right shots, keep working on the shots, I think eventually they’re gonna fall sooner than later.”

On the NBA’s best shooters’ slumps:

“It happens. It happens to the best of them because everybody is definitely human and every human has their ups and their downs when it comes to shooting. That’s why we have to keep embracing the little things, because they’re not gonna always fall.”

On Landry Shamet’s natural ability to create opportunities through off-ball movement:

“You could drill it, and guys will pick up on it, but you can tell (Shamet) is a natural with it.”

On the explanation for his unusually poor shooting percentages to start the season:

“Missing shots. I normally make.”

On whether his offseason wrist surgery has affected his shooting:

On Landry Shamet’s ability to create defensive closeouts:

“He creates great closeouts, whether he’s shooting or catching. He has a good knack for it.

“It’s just how he operates. He just finds the right windows, whether it’s benefiting him or someone else.”

On Jordan Clarkson’s role:

“He has a professionalism about it. For a person who is willing to do that — he makes our team better. Great person, great teammate. Off the court, he’s a great dude and someone I enjoy being around.”

On why the Knicks’ defense has been ahead of their offense early in the season:

“We have great coaches. [Brendan O’Connor] and [Darren Erman], they do a great job indicating to us what we need to be doing on the court, and then guys are executing defensively and we’re getting stops. That’s always our goal.

“We don’t think about it. Even when you said that, I didn’t think about it. There’s always room for improvement though, so always striving for better.”

On the Knicks finally increasing their pace:

“We finally played fast. We’ve been playing very slow, very stagnant. We finally got out, we ran.”

On the champion Knicks remaining a work in progress:

“It’s early in the season. I think everything’s a work in progress. Last year, I feel like we probably hit our best stride in the playoffs. So we were a work in progress the whole year. That’s the nature of the NBA season. You gotta keep getting better each and every day, each and every game, and be ready to go.”

On the Knicks’ dissatisfaction with their start to the season:

“I just think we’ve got to win, and I think it’s still early in the season, and I don’t think anybody in this locker room is satisfied with where we’re at. Happy to be in the win column tonight, but, you know, to point to 10 things offensively and defensively that we need to improve on. So the good news is there’s no panic there. Some nights right now, it might be the offense ahead of the defense and vice versa. We’ve had a hard time making shots so far early in the season. Tonight a few went in, but then we had some slippage defensively. So, a little give and take, but luckily that’s not the point. The point is for us to continue to get better and we’ll continue to do that.”

On Mike Brown holding the Knicks accountable and not allowing the Nets win to disguise their problems:

“We have to be real with ourselves. And Mike’s great with that, assesses things in film, calls it as it is. Our group’s great with that. We all understand that by no means — we’re not taking this as any potential fool’s gold. The whole goal right now is to continue to get better, and we want to do that. So that’s the thought process.”

On learning to move without the basketball by playing three-on-three without dribbling as a child:

“I remember growing up playing full-court three-on-three with no dribble, so you just learn how to move without the ball. I’m lucky I had that implemented for me at a young age. I wish more kids and hope more kids would do that moving forward in today’s game. I think it really helps you learn how to play and understand how to move and get open. So, it’s kinda always been something I’ve tried to continue to get better at.”

items.title: Game Preview: Knicks vs. Bulls, November 4, 2026
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
One of the most dreaded speeches a head basketball coach has to make is the one where he talks up an obviously overmatched opponent. He knows the other squad will have plenty of trouble hanging with his ball club even on a good night. On a regular night, his troops would trash the opposition worse than the Globetrotters ever did the Washington Generals. Yet he also knows that complacency can ruin the best game plan and that arrogance has led many teams down the road to hell. Luckily for Mike Brown, he has recent history on his side for his pep talk about the Chicago Bulls.

Those very ballers nearly pulled off the upset against your world champions Knicks last week. Although it came on a second night of a back-to-back and in the not-so-friendly confines of the United Center, the warning should still resonate with the Bockers before they host one of the league’s worst teams. Even if you could argue there isn’t anybody worse than Thiago Splitter’s young group so far this year.

Sitting at the bottom of the league at 1–6, the Bulls have already lost games by 19, 35, and 43 points and sport the worst point differential in the NBA. Yes, even the Sacramento Acuffs have Chicago beat in that regard. While the offense at times actually looks serviceable, the defense has been nothing short of abysmal. They allow 128.8 points per contest, and games against them regularly turn into a shootaround for the opposition. Defending downtown has been especially tough, with teams nailing almost 40 percent of their long-range shots against Chicago. Yes, they’ve faced some stiff competition, but come on.

Bulls come to MSG on a 5-game losing streak

People in the Windy City are fairly relaxed, though. With a new coach and a young star in the fold, 2026–27 was always going to be a rebuilding year, one they sorely needed after what felt like a decade of drowning in mediocrity. Caleb Wilson, the fourth overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, has been as good as advertised early on and finally gives Chicago fans something to look forward to. The former UNC highflyer is hardly efficient yet, makes plenty of rookie mistakes, and at times doesn’t really know what this basketball thing is that he’s doing out there. But man, does his game look promising.

Wilson is an ultra-modern combo forward with world-class athleticism and a good, determined head on his shoulders. He plays extremely hard, looks to be enjoying himself a ton out there, and seems to possess a drive you usually find only in the cream of the NBA’s crop. If he adds a few pounds and works on his jumper, it’s easy to see the 20-year-old becoming the centerpiece of whatever the Bulls envision for their future.

The same can’t be said for Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis, also two promising young players who have struggled under new head coach Thiago Splitter. Giddey’s scoring has dropped from 17 points per game last season to just nine this year, and he’s shooting south of 37 percent from the field. Rumor has it a wrist injury is hampering the Australian, and it might be a problem all year.

Plenty of young Bulls are struggling

Buzelis’ excuse is that he’s struggled out of the gate before. But even with a world of athletic talent and plenty of promise, he sometimes looks like one of those players who will never really put it all together. It’s still way too early to give up on a 22-year-old as gifted as the former G League Ignite hooper. At some point, though, those gifts have to show up night in and night out on the NBA hardwood, well after the layup line.

Chicago’s most accomplished veteran, Norman Powell, should help in that regard, but how much he can do is debatable. He probably hasn’t even unpacked his suitcase yet, and he’ll most likely be shipped out to a wannabe contender by the trade deadline. Is someone like that really going to change your culture? Powell has played very good ball for years, but can he be the guy who turns things around in Chicago? Your guess is as good as mine.

Even if Powell is exactly the vet presence Bulls ownership envisions, Splitter is still fighting an uphill battle. The roster is extremely young and short on inside brawn (sorry, Stix Smith, Zach Collins, and Nic “I can’t lose to the Knicks” Claxton), reliable outside shooting, and any sort of cohesiveness. The losses should pile up pretty quickly. The Knicks should help their former rivals along and get back to .500 in this one. Anything else would be unacceptable.

But I’m sure Mike Brown will remind his team of that in his pregame speech.

Who: New York Knicks (3-4) vs Chicago Bulls (1-6)Date: Wednesday, November 4, 2026Place: Madison Square Garden, NYCFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

items.title: Player Grades: Knicks 103, Nets 90
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
For three quarters Monday night, the Knicks looked like they might actually lose to the Nets. The Nets? The last place Nets? While we might get apoplectic, the champs seemed unconcerned about falling behind. When they finally flipped the switch, they turned a 79–75 deficit into a 103–90 win, outscoring Brooklyn 28–11 in the fourth at the Garden. That’s 15 straight wins against the neighbors. Landry Shamet did a lot of the work to make it so.

22 points (6–8 FG, 4–6 3PT, 6–6 FT), 1 rebound, 1 assist in 30 minutes

On a night when the starters happily hurled threes like pre-teens playing Pop Shot, Shamet sank a steady four of six, plus every free throw he took. His season-high 22 kept the Knicks in it long enough for the rest of them to wake up.

While the Knicks spun their wheels in third-quarter mud, Josh Hart collected his fourth foul with a lotta game remaining. Shamet replaced him at 8:44 and scored six points on perfect shooting from downtown. The first, at 2:26, cut Brooklyn’s lead to a single point; the second, with a minute left, made it 77-75. According to Basketball Reference, he had a team-high game score of 19.4. Pretty good for a sub.

8 points (3–6 FG, 2–5 3PT), 6 rebounds, 7 assists, 3 steals in 27 minutes (+22)

Hart had a crooked finger in just about everything that made the fourth quarter exciting. In that final frame, he hit a Kolek-assisted three to pull the Knicks within one, then assisted on back-to-back Anunoby threes and a Kolek layup (everybody seems to enjoy playing with Tyler, don’t they?). Josh intercepted a Julius Randle pass and took it the other way for a layup. His grade suffers for taking just six shots and collecting six fouls, but maybe he deserves a little more love for being a team high +22?

18 points (4–10 FG, 3–7 3PT, 7–8 FT), 4 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 steals in 38 minutes

OG played 38 minutes, got to the line eight times, and hit back-to-back threes in the fourth when the Knicks finally started to put Brooklyn away. Seven free throws will do a lot for a night when only four shots fall from the floor. Give credit to his stamina: after bumping bodies with that bull Julius Randle all night, he still had gas in the tank to help his team in the fourth. He hit the go-ahead three at 10:29 and another bomb 28 seconds later to make it 84–79. He also set up Clarkson’s transition three. Loses points for still struggling to finish at the rim.

11 points (4–11 FG, 1–4 3PT), 16 rebounds, 5 assists in 35 minutes

A weird game for Karl-Anthony. He had double-digit rebounds in the first half, but zero points. After intermission, he scraped together 11 points with much more aggressive drives to the rim. As New York rallied in the fourth, he banked in a short fadeaway, grabbed three defensive boards, and found Landry Shamet for the Knicks’ final basket. His back up, Andre Drummond, grabbed nine boards in his 13 minutes, but dividing the workload between the pair is unsustainable. James Wiseman is glued to the bench. Leon, what’s your move?

19 points (6–16 FG, 4–11 3PT, 3–6 FT), 2 rebounds, 6 assists in 33.5 minutes

Four threes and six assists are dandy, but missing half his free-throws and ten field goal attempts had us a little worried. He’s been mostly automatic since coming to New York, so forgive us for jumping to conclusions like: maybe he should spend less time doing extracurricular activities and more in the gym? He started off the game great, making 3-of-4 from deep, but then disappeared for a while.

7 points (3–5 FG, 1–2 3PT) in 11 minutes (+17)

Some guys can do a lot in 11 minutes. Clarkson squeezed seven points into his sliver of time (entirely in the second half) and was still a +17. As the fourth quarter started, a game that had been a nuisance all night was finally starting to break open. Jordan blocked Nolan Traoré’s layup and hit a transition three seven seconds later to push the lead to 10. He added a floater at 4:00 to keep the momentum going. He loses a point for collecting two fouls and a technical foul in the span of a minute during the third period, which didn’t help matters while the team was flailing.

After the game, coach Mike Brown offered high praise for the vet. “I’ve been around some good teammates when it comes to players. He’s gotta be the best. He’s the definition of ultimate pro,” he said. “You have a veteran that’s been there, done that, and he’s willing to accept the role that most guys wouldn’t accept […]. And he’s willing to accept it… and still try to uplift everybody and connect everybody while he’s going through what he’s going through. That’s the ultimate team player.”

6 points (2–4 FG, 2–4 3PT), 1 rebound, 2 assists in 16.5 minutes

Deuce hit two of four from deep and added a couple of assists. A decent shift on a night when the Knicks could’ve used a few more of those. Two steals is great. Four shots in almost 17 minutes seems insufficient, however.

6 points (1–7 FG, 0–2 3PT, 4–4 FT), 2 rebounds in 16 minutes (−11)

Hoo boy. Bridges made one shot from the floor and did little on defense to make up for it. The Knicks lost his 16 minutes by 11 points, the worst mark in the rotation. At least he got to the foul line for the first time after six games. 

It’s perhaps too soon to sound the panic alarm, but he has shot 16 of 52 for the season. Mike Brown has taken notice. He ended Kal’s night after just a few minutes into the third quarter, and when he sent the starters back at the end of the game, Shamet took Bridges’ spot. 

The Knicks got away with three quarters of sleepwalking because Shamet kept them close and Hart, OG, and the bench gave them life in the fourth. Next up are the Bulls on Wednesday. In their first meeting of the season, last week, the Knicks won but needed 48 points from the bench to bail them out. Do we see a trend emerging?
